journal_name: ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework termed Quantum-Inspired Reconfigurable Computing (QIRC) that fundamentally reimagines the architectural design space for field-programmable gate arrays. Unlike conventional static reconfiguration models, QIRC establishes a mathematical foundation based on probabilistic state transitions and superposition-inspired resource allocation. We formalize the reconfiguration problem as a constrained optimization problem over a hypergraph representation of computational tasks, enabling the systematic exploration of configuration states that simultaneously satisfy multiple performance objectives. The theoretical analysis proves that QIRC achieves a computational complexity reduction from O(n²) to O(n log n) for configuration scheduling in coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of latent configuration spaces, which represent implicit parallelism within reconfigurable fabrics that traditional compilation flows fail to exploit. Experimental validation through analytical modeling demonstrates that QIRC enables a 3.7× improvement in configuration throughput compared to state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining deterministic timing guarantees. This work establishes reconfigurable computing as a new computational paradigm that transcends the hardware/software boundary, providing theoretical foundations for future generations of adaptive computing systems.

This paper presents an enhanced analytical model for predicting and optimizing communication overhead in heterogeneous computing systems with reconfigurable accelerators. Building upon the traditional roofline model, we introduce the Reconfigurable Roofline Extension (RRE) that incorporates dynamic reconfiguration costs and FPGA memory bandwidth variability. The RRE model accounts for run-time reconfiguration latency, partial configuration overhead, and the temporal characteristics of configuration bitstream delivery through a novel analytical framework termed Communication-Aware Reconfiguration Cost (CARC). We derive closed-form expressions for predicting performance degradation due to reconfiguration and provide formal proofs establishing the bounds of estimation accuracy. The model enables accurate prediction of effective throughput for applications with frequent reconfiguration, achieving a prediction error below 8% compared to 34% error for the baseline roofline model. We demonstrate the practical utility of RRE through case studies in high-level synthesis optimization, where the model guides configuration parameter selection to maximize hardware utilization. This work significantly advances the theoretical toolkit available for reconfigurable system design, enabling architects to make informed decisions regarding hardware/software co-design trade-offs with quantifiable performance guarantees.

This paper presents Configurable Mesh Reconfigurable Interconnect (CMRI), a revolutionary interconnect architecture for coarse-grained reconfigurable arrays that enables runtime-reconfigurable communication topology. Unlike traditional mesh-based interconnects with fixed routing paths, CMRI employs a novel programmable crossbar fabric at each processing element that can dynamically establish arbitrary connection patterns without reconfiguration latency overhead. The system architecture introduces hierarchical configuration domains that allow simultaneous reconfiguration of different interconnect regions while maintaining operational continuity in unaffected areas. We implement a complete prototype on 28nm FPGA technology demonstrating 512 processing elements with 2.4 Tb/s aggregate interconnect bandwidth. The CMRI system achieves a 4.2× improvement in average application performance compared to conventional mesh interconnects for dataflow-intensive workloads, while reducing dynamic power consumption by 38% through intelligent path allocation. The design includes a novel configuration controller that supports both compile-time and run-time topology adaptation, enabling applications to evolve their communication patterns based on data characteristics. This work fundamentally changes how we conceptualize reconfigurable interconnects, transforming them from static infrastructure into active computational resources that participate in adaptive computing.

This paper presents RTHLS (Runtime-Targeted High-Level Synthesis), an improved high-level synthesis framework that generates hardware designs optimized for run-time reconfiguration scenarios. Existing HLS tools treat reconfiguration as an afterthought, generating configuration bitstreams that exhibit suboptimal reconfiguration efficiency. RTHLS introduces configuration-aware synthesis that explicitly optimizes for reconfiguration latency by analyzing the temporal locality of configuration access patterns. The framework incorporates three novel optimizations: (1) configuration compression using application-specific dictionaries, (2) incremental partial configuration scheduling, and (3) configuration prefetching guided by dataflow analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RTHLS through comprehensive evaluation on a suite of 24 benchmark applications spanning signal processing, machine learning inference, and scientific computing domains. Results indicate that designs synthesized with RTHLS achieve an average reconfiguration speedup of 2.8× compared to standard HLS flows, while maintaining comparable computational performance. The framework adds an average of 6% hardware overhead for configuration infrastructure, which is amortized within 3-5 reconfiguration cycles for the evaluated workloads. RTHLS integrates seamlessly with existing FPGA design flows, providing a practical path for hardware/software co-design that accounts for the unique characteristics of reconfigurable systems.
